<!-- remark-1: body_md -->
\label{rem:normalisation}
  The Bernstein polynomials often used in the literature instead of barycentric monomials include the multinomial factor
  $|\alpha|! / (\alpha_0 ! \cdots \alpha_D !)$, which is invariant under any permutation of the entries
  of $\alpha$. Statements whose formulas only permute the entries of $\alpha$, which
  covers the calculus related to $\mathcal{P}_r\Lambda^1$, therefore hold for the Bernstein basis.
  However, the calculus related to $\mathcal{P}_r^{-}\Lambda^1$ transfers one unit of degree between entries
  of $\alpha$. The multinomial factor then fails to cancel, introducing ratios of multinomials in the change matrices instead of $\pm 1$. We work
  with bare monomials throughout. The Bernstein counterpart of the trimmed
  calculus is worked out in Apdx.~\ref{sec:bernstein}.
<!-- end remark-1 -->
<!-- lemma-1: body_md -->
\label{lem:bernstein}
  For every multi-exponent $\beta$,
  \begin{equation}
    A_{\pi^{-1}}^* (b(\xi; \beta)) = b(\lambda; \pi(\beta)), \qquad A_\pi^* (b(\lambda; \beta)) = b(\xi; \pi^{-1}(\beta)).
  \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-1 -->
<!-- proof-1: body_md -->
By \eqref{eq:relabel}, $\xi^\beta = \prod_i \xi_i^{\beta_i} = \prod_i \lambda_{\pi(i)}^{\beta_i}
  = \prod_j \lambda_j^{\beta_{\pi^{-1}(j)}} = \lambda^{\pi(\beta)}$. The second identity is the first with
  $\pi \leftarrow \pi^{-1}$.
<!-- end proof-1 -->
<!-- theorem-1: body_md -->
\label{thm:conformity-reduction}
  Let $K_+ = \Phi_\xi (\Delta)$ and $K_- = \Phi_\lambda (\Delta)$ share the face $F = \Phi_\xi (f_+) = \Phi_\lambda (f_-)$,
  where $f_\pm$ are faces of $\Delta$. Choose $\pi \in S_{D+1}$ such that
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:pi-compat}
    \Phi_\lambda (v_{\pi(i)}) = \Phi_\xi (v_i) \quad \text{for all } i \in f_+
  \end{equation}
  (such $\pi$ exist, and satisfy $\pi(f_+) = f_-$). Then, for $\hat{u}_+, \hat{u}_- \in \Lambda^1 (\Delta)$,
  the traces on $F$ of $u_+ = (\Phi_\xi^{-1})^* \hat{u}_+$ and
  $u_- = (\Phi_\lambda^{-1})^* \hat{u}_-$ coincide if and only if
  \begin{equation}
    \operatorname{tr}_{f_-} \hat{u}_- = \operatorname{tr}_{f_-} (A_{\pi^{-1}}^* \hat{u}_+).
  \end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-1 -->
<!-- proof-2: body_md -->
The pullback operation commutes with the restriction to subsimplices, so
  \[ \operatorname{tr}_F u_+ = (\Phi_\xi|_{f_+}^{-1})^* \operatorname{tr}_{f_+} \hat{u}_+, \qquad
     \operatorname{tr}_F u_- = (\Phi_\lambda|_{f_-}^{-1})^* \operatorname{tr}_{f_-} \hat{u}_-. \]
  Hence $\operatorname{tr}_F u_+ = \operatorname{tr}_F u_-$ iff
  $\operatorname{tr}_{f_-} \hat{u}_- = \theta^* \operatorname{tr}_{f_+} \hat{u}_+$ with
  $\theta = \Phi_\xi|_{f_+}^{-1} \circ \Phi_\lambda|_{f_-} : f_- \to f_+$. By \eqref{eq:pi-compat},
  $\Phi_\xi = \Phi_\lambda \circ A_\pi$ on $f_+$, so $\theta = A_\pi^{-1}|_{f_-}$, and
  $\theta^* \operatorname{tr}_{f_+} \hat{u}_+ = \operatorname{tr}_{f_-} (A_{\pi^{-1}}^* \hat{u}_+)$.
<!-- end proof-2 -->
<!-- remark-2: body_md -->
The permutation $\pi$ in \eqref{eq:pi-compat} is only determined on $f_+$ and is arbitrary
  elsewhere. This is not an issue since the basis functions owned by a face $f \subseteq f_+$
  will be indexed by data supported on $f$ (Sects.~\ref{sec:full} and~\ref{sec:trimmed}), so the relabelling actions on them depend on $\pi$ only through its restriction to $f_+$.
<!-- end remark-2 -->
<!-- definition-1: body_md -->
\label{def:psi}
  Let $f$ be a face of $\Delta$ with $\dim f \geq 1$, let $k \in f$, and let
  $s \in \{0, 1\}^{D+1}$ be an indicator vector with $\operatorname{supp}(s) \cup \{k\} = f$. The
  associated directional 1-form is
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:psi}
    \psi(\xi; f, k, s) = \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_k - \frac{s_k}{|s|} \sum_{j \in f} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_j.
  \end{equation}
<!-- end definition-1 -->
<!-- definition-2: body_md -->
\label{def:spanning}
  $\mathcal{S}(\Delta_\xi, r)$ is the set of triplets $(f, k, \alpha)$ with $\dim f \geq 1$, $k \in f$,
  $|\alpha| = r$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha) \cup \{k\} = f$. To each triplet is associated the 1-form
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:w}
    w(\xi; f, k, \alpha) = b(\xi; \alpha) \, \psi(\xi; f, k, \mathds{1}_{\alpha}).
  \end{equation}
  The first shape of \eqref{eq:psi-shapes}
  occurs iff $\alpha_k > 0$ and the second iff $\alpha_k = 0$.
<!-- end definition-2 -->
<!-- remark-3: body_md -->
The directional forms of Arnold, Falk and Winther are weighted by the exponent
  \emph{values}, namely $\psi_k^{\alpha, f} = \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_k - (\alpha_k / |\alpha|) \sum_{j \in f} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_j$
  \cite[eq.~(8.2)]{ArnoldFalkWinther2009}. Replacing the support indicator
  $(\mathds{1}_{\alpha})_k / |\mathds{1}_{\alpha}|$ by the weight $\alpha_k / |\alpha|$ preserves the two cases of \eqref{eq:psi-shapes}, but makes
  it fully depend on $\alpha$, including the order $r = |\alpha|$. On the other hand, the directional
  forms \eqref{eq:psi} constitute an $r$-independent \emph{catalogue}
  (Definition~\ref{def:catalog}) that is sufficient to assemble the polynomial set and basis. The upcoming relabelling theorems still apply to the bases from \cite{ArnoldFalkWinther2009} for two main reasons, that
  the weight commutes with relabelling,
  $(\mathds{1}_{\pi(\alpha)})_{\pi(k)} = (\mathds{1}_{\alpha})_k$ and
  $(\pi(\alpha))_{\pi(k)} / |\pi(\alpha)| = \alpha_k / |\alpha|$, and that the weights over the face
  sum to one.
<!-- end remark-3 -->
<!-- theorem-2: body_md -->
\label{thm:spanning}
  $\operatorname{span} \mathcal{S}(\Delta_\xi, r) = \mathcal{P}_r\Lambda^1 (\Delta)$ for every $r \geq 1$.
<!-- end theorem-2 -->
<!-- proof-3: body_md -->
The inclusion $\operatorname{span} \mathcal{S}(\Delta_\xi, r) \subseteq \mathcal{P}_r\Lambda^1 (\Delta)$ is straightforward,
  since every $w(\xi; f, k, \alpha)$ is a combination of the generators
  $\xi^\alpha \, \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_j$ of \eqref{eq:full-space}. For the converse inclusion, by
  \eqref{eq:full-space} it suffices to express each form $\xi^\alpha \, \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_i$
  with $|\alpha| = r$ in $\operatorname{span} \mathcal{S}$. Given such a form, we set
  $f = \operatorname{supp}(\alpha) \cup \{i\}$ and distinguish three cases.

  Assume first that $\alpha_i = 0$. Then $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha) = f \setminus i$, and $|f| \geq 2$ because
  $r \geq 1$ forces $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha) \neq \emptyset$. The second shape of \eqref{eq:psi-shapes} gives
  $\psi(\xi; f, i, \mathds{1}_{\alpha}) = \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_i$, and therefore
  $\xi^\alpha \, \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_i = w(\xi; f, i, \alpha)$ belongs to the spanning set.

  Assume next that $\alpha_i > 0$ and $|f| = 1$. Then $\alpha = r \, 1_i$, and the
  ambient relation \eqref{eq:ambient-relation} yields
  $\xi^\alpha \, \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_i = - \sum_{j \neq i} \xi^\alpha \, \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_j$. Every summand on the
  right has $\alpha_j = 0$, so it is covered by the first case.

  Assume finally that $\alpha_i > 0$ and $|f| \geq 2$. Then $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha) = f$, and the
  first shape of \eqref{eq:psi-shapes} yields, after multiplication by $\xi^\alpha$ and
  rearrangement,
  \begin{equation}
    \xi^\alpha \, \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_i = w(\xi; f, i, \alpha) + \frac{1}{|f|} \xi^\alpha \sum_{j \in f} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_j
    = w(\xi; f, i, \alpha) - \frac{1}{|f|} \sum_{j \notin f} \xi^\alpha \, \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_j,
  \end{equation}
  where the last equality uses \eqref{eq:ambient-relation} in the form
  $\sum_{j \in f} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_j = - \sum_{j \notin f} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_j$. Every term of the last sum has
  $j \notin f = \operatorname{supp}(\alpha)$, so it is covered by the first case, and the proof is
  complete.
<!-- end proof-3 -->
<!-- remark-4: body_md -->
We require $r \geq 1$ throughout. $\mathcal{P}_0 \Lambda^1$ admits no face-owned
  geometric decomposition for $D \geq 2$, because the edge-owned functions alone would number $\binom{D+1}{2} > D = \dim \mathcal{P}_0 \Lambda^1$. Note that
  $\mathcal{S}(\Delta_\xi, 0) = \emptyset$.
<!-- end remark-4 -->
<!-- definition-3: body_md -->
\label{def:filter}
  The directional form $\psi(\xi; f, k, s)$ is \emph{anchored} if
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:filter}
    s_i = 0 \quad \text{for all} \quad i < \min(f \setminus k).
  \end{equation}
  $\mathcal{B}(\Delta_\xi, r)$ is defined to be the set of triplets $(f, k, \alpha) \in \mathcal{S}(\Delta_\xi, r)$ whose
  directional factor $\psi(\xi; f, k, \mathds{1}_{\alpha})$ is anchored.
<!-- end definition-3 -->
<!-- theorem-3: body_md -->
\label{thm:U1}
  The directional form $\psi(\xi; f, k, s)$ fails to be anchored if and only
  if $\operatorname{supp}(s) = f$ and $k = \min f$. In particular, a triplet
  $(f, k, \alpha) \in \mathcal{S}(\Delta_\xi, r)$ lies in $\mathcal{B}(\Delta_\xi, r)$ if and only if
  $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha) \neq f$ or $k \neq \min f$.
<!-- end theorem-3 -->
<!-- proof-4: body_md -->
If $\operatorname{supp}(s) \neq f$, then $\operatorname{supp}(s) = f \setminus k$, so
  $\min(f \setminus k) = \min \operatorname{supp}(s)$ and every $i \in \operatorname{supp}(s)$ satisfies
  $i \geq \min(f \setminus k)$, so that \eqref{eq:filter} holds. If $\operatorname{supp}(s) = f$ and
  $k > \min f$, then $\min(f \setminus k) = \min f = \min \operatorname{supp}(s)$ and the same argument
  applies. If $\operatorname{supp}(s) = f$ and $k = \min f$, then $s_{\min f} = 1$ with
  $\min f < \min(f \setminus k)$, violating \eqref{eq:filter}. The triplet statement follows
  with $s = \mathds{1}_{\alpha}$, since $\operatorname{supp}(\mathds{1}_{\alpha}) = \operatorname{supp}(\alpha)$.
<!-- end proof-4 -->
<!-- definition-4: body_md -->
\label{def:catalog}
  The \emph{directional catalogue} $\Psi(\Delta_\xi)$ is the family of anchored directional
  forms, indexed by their arguments $(f, k, s)$.
<!-- end definition-4 -->
<!-- remark-5: body_md -->
The catalogue is not a set since some of its elements may be
  identical. The second shape of \eqref{eq:psi-shapes} does not depend on $f$ or $s$,
  so any two faces containing $k$ contribute the same form $\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_k$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:U1}, for each face $f$ the catalogue contains the
  $2 \dim f + 1$ forms with $\operatorname{supp}(s) = f \setminus k$, $k \in f$, and with
  $\operatorname{supp}(s) = f$, $k \in f \setminus \min f$. The catalogue is finite and $r$-independent.
<!-- end remark-5 -->
<!-- lemma-2: body_md -->
\label{lem:psi-resummation}
  Let $\operatorname{supp}(s) = f$ and $k \in f$. Then
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:psi-resummation}
    \psi(\xi; f, k, s) = - \sum_{v \in f \setminus k} \psi(\xi; f, v, s).
  \end{equation}
  Additionally, every summand in the right-hand side is anchored when $k = \min f$.
<!-- end lemma-2 -->
<!-- proof-5: body_md -->
Since $\operatorname{supp}(s) = f$, $(f, v, s)$ are valid parameters of $\psi$ for every $v \in f$. By
  \eqref{eq:psi-shapes}, $\psi(\xi; f, v, s) = \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_v - \frac{1}{|f|} \sum_{j \in f} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_j$.
  Summing over $v \in f \setminus k$,
  \begin{equation}
    \sum_{v \in f \setminus k} \psi(\xi; f, v, s)
    = \sum_{v \in f \setminus k} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_v - \frac{|f| - 1}{|f|} \sum_{j \in f} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_j
    = - \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_k + \frac{1}{|f|} \sum_{j \in f} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_j
    = - \psi(\xi; f, k, s).
  \end{equation}
  For $k = \min f$, each $(f, v, s)$ with $v \in f \setminus \min f$ is anchored by
  Theorem~\ref{thm:U1}.
<!-- end proof-5 -->
<!-- theorem-4: body_md -->
\label{thm:U2}
  Let $(f, k, \alpha) \in \mathcal{S}(\Delta_\xi, r) \setminus \mathcal{B}(\Delta_\xi, r)$, i.e., $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha) = f$ and $k = \min f$.
  Then
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:resummation}
    w(\xi; f, k, \alpha) = - \sum_{v \in f \setminus k} w(\xi; f, v, \alpha),
  \end{equation}
  where every triplet $(f, v, \alpha)$ for $v \in f \setminus k$ belongs to
  $\mathcal{B}(\Delta_\xi, r)$.
<!-- end theorem-4 -->
<!-- proof-6: body_md -->
Multiply \eqref{eq:psi-resummation}, at $s = \mathds{1}_{\alpha}$, by $b(\xi; \alpha)$. The summands belong to $\mathcal{B}$ since their directional forms are anchored as in Lemma~\ref{lem:psi-resummation}.
<!-- end proof-6 -->
<!-- lemma-3: body_md -->
\label{lem:count}
  For a face $f$ with $d = \dim f$, the triplets of $\mathcal{B}(\Delta_\xi, r)$ owned by $f$
  number $(r + 1) \binom{r - 1}{d - 1}$, and in total
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:count}
    \# \mathcal{B}(\Delta_\xi, r) = D \binom{r + D}{D} = \dim \mathcal{P}_r\Lambda^1.
  \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-3 -->
<!-- proof-7: body_md -->
Fix $f$ with $|f| = d + 1$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:U1} the elements of $\mathcal{B}$ owned by $f$
  are: (a) $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha) = f \setminus k$ with $k \in f$ arbitrary, giving $(d+1)$ choices of $k$
  times the number of multi-exponents $\alpha$ with $|\alpha| = r$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha) = f \setminus k$, that is, of ways of writing $r$ as an ordered sum of $d$ positive integers, which is $\binom{r - 1}{d - 1}$; and (b) $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha) = f$ with $k \in f \setminus \min f$, giving
  $d$ choices of $k$ times the $\binom{r - 1}{d}$ multi-exponents with $|\alpha| = r$ and $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha) = f$.
  The absorption identity $d \binom{r - 1}{d} = (r - d) \binom{r - 1}{d - 1}$
  collapses this count to
  \[ (d + 1) \binom{r - 1}{d - 1} + d \binom{r - 1}{d} = (r + 1) \binom{r - 1}{d - 1}, \]
  which is the dimension of the space of 1-forms of degree $r$ on a $d$-simplex
  with vanishing trace on its boundary
  \cite[Corollary 5.2 and eq.~(3.7)]{ArnoldFalkWinther2009}.
  The geometric decomposition of \cite[Section 8]{ArnoldFalkWinther2009} expresses
  $\mathcal{P}_r\Lambda^1$ as the direct sum of those spaces over the faces of $\Delta_\xi$, so summing
  over the $\binom{D + 1}{d + 1}$ faces of each dimension gives
  \[ \# \mathcal{B}(\Delta_\xi, r) = \sum_{d = 1}^{D} \binom{D + 1}{d + 1} \, (r + 1) \binom{r - 1}{d - 1} = \dim \mathcal{P}_r\Lambda^1. \]
<!-- end proof-7 -->
<!-- corollary-1: body_md -->
\label{cor:basis}
  $\mathcal{B}(\Delta_\xi, r)$ is a basis of $\mathcal{P}_r\Lambda^1 (\Delta)$.
<!-- end corollary-1 -->
<!-- proof-8: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:U2} every element of $\mathcal{S} \setminus \mathcal{B}$ lies in $\operatorname{span} \mathcal{B}$, so
  $\operatorname{span} \mathcal{B} = \operatorname{span} \mathcal{S} = \mathcal{P}_r\Lambda^1$ by Theorem~\ref{thm:spanning}. By Lemma~\ref{lem:count} the
  spanning family $\mathcal{B}$ has cardinality $\dim \mathcal{P}_r\Lambda^1$, hence is a basis. In particular, distinct triplets of $\mathcal{B}(\Delta_\xi, r)$ give distinct forms.
<!-- end proof-8 -->
<!-- remark-6: body_md -->
The index set of $\mathcal{B}(\Delta_\xi, r)$ is that of the basis of $\mathcal{P}_r\Lambda^1$ in \cite[Section 9]{ArnoldFalkWinther2009}, whose anchoring condition is \eqref{eq:filter}, and its cardinality is computed there as well; only the weight in the directional forms differs. Since the functions differ, spanning has to be established for the present basis, which is what Theorem~\ref{thm:U2} and Lemma~\ref{lem:count} do.
<!-- end remark-6 -->
<!-- lemma-4: body_md -->
\label{lem:trace}
  Let $(f, k, \alpha) \in \mathcal{S}(\Delta_\xi, r)$ and let $g$ be a face of $\Delta_\xi$ that does not
  contain $f$. Then $\operatorname{tr}_g w(\xi; f, k, \alpha) = 0$.
<!-- end lemma-4 -->
<!-- proof-9: body_md -->
Since $f = \operatorname{supp}(\alpha) \cup \{k\}$ is not contained in $g$, some label $i$ of $f$ lies outside $g$, and $\xi_i$ vanishes identically on $g$. If $i \in \operatorname{supp}(\alpha)$, the monomial $b(\xi; \alpha)$ vanishes on $g$ and so does the trace. Otherwise $i = k$ with $\alpha_k = 0$, the second shape of \eqref{eq:psi-shapes} gives $\psi(\xi; f, k, \mathds{1}_{\alpha}) = \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_k$, and $\operatorname{tr}_g \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_k = 0$ because $\xi_k$ vanishes on $g$.
<!-- end proof-9 -->
<!-- remark-7: body_md -->
\label{rem:extension}
  For faces $f \subseteq g$, let $E_{f, g}$ be the barycentric extension of \cite[Section 2.3]{ArnoldFalkWinther2009}: an expression in the barycentric coordinates of $f$ is read as the same expression in those of $g$, so that $\operatorname{tr}_f E_{f, g} = \mathrm{id}$. Since \eqref{eq:w} involves only the labels of $f$, every basis function owned by $f$ is the barycentric extension of its trace on $f$. Those traces are the elements of $\mathcal{B}(f, r)$ whose face is $f$ itself. They are a subfamily of a basis of $\mathcal{P}_r\Lambda^1(f)$, by Corollary~\ref{cor:basis} applied on the simplex $f$, hence linearly independent, and by Lemma~\ref{lem:trace} applied on $f$ they have zero trace on every proper face of $f$. They therefore lie in the bubble space of $f$, the subspace of $\mathcal{P}_r\Lambda^1(f)$ with vanishing trace on $\partial f$, whose dimension $(r + 1) \binom{r - 1}{d - 1}$ equals their number by Lemma~\ref{lem:count}, so they form a basis of it. Together with Lemma~\ref{lem:trace},
  this makes $\mathcal{B}(\Delta_\xi, r)$ a geometrically decomposed basis in the sense of
  \cite[Section 4]{ArnoldFalkWinther2009}.
<!-- end remark-7 -->
<!-- lemma-5: body_md -->
\label{lem:psi-equivariance}
  For every admissible argument of Definition~\ref{def:psi} and every $\pi \in S_{D+1}$,
  \begin{equation}
    A_{\pi^{-1}}^* (\psi(\xi; f, k, s)) = \psi(\lambda; \pi(f), \pi(k), \pi(s)).
  \end{equation}
  In particular
  $A_{\pi^{-1}}^* (\psi(\xi; f, k, \mathds{1}_{\alpha})) = \psi(\lambda; \pi(f), \pi(k), \mathds{1}_{\pi(\alpha)})$,
  by the identity $\mathds{1}_{\pi(\alpha)} = \pi(\mathds{1}_{\alpha})$ of Sect.~\ref{sec:prelim-simplex}.
<!-- end lemma-5 -->
<!-- proof-10: body_md -->
The pullback $A_{\pi^{-1}}^*$ maps $\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_k \mapsto \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \lambda_{\pi(k)}$ and
  $\sum_{j \in f} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_j \mapsto \sum_{j \in \pi(f)} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \lambda_j$. Moreover
  $\pi(s)_{\pi(k)} = s_k$ and $|\pi(s)| = |s|$, so the weight in \eqref{eq:psi} is
  unchanged.
<!-- end proof-10 -->
<!-- theorem-5: body_md -->
\label{thm:psi-pullback}
  Let $\psi(\xi; f, k, s)$ be anchored and let $\pi \in S_{D+1}$. Then
  $(\pi(f), \pi(k), \pi(s))$ is an admissible argument of Definition~\ref{def:psi} and exactly one of the following
  holds.
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \emph{Relabelled}. If $s_k = 0$ or $\pi(k) \neq \min \pi(f)$, then
    $\psi(\lambda; \pi(f), \pi(k), \pi(s))$ is anchored and
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:psi-pullback-single}
      A_{\pi^{-1}}^* (\psi(\xi; f, k, s)) = \psi(\lambda; \pi(f), \pi(k), \pi(s)).
    \end{equation}
  \item \emph{Filter hit.} If $s_k = 1$ and $\pi(k) = \min \pi(f)$, then
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:psi-pullback-hit}
      A_{\pi^{-1}}^* (\psi(\xi; f, k, s)) = - \sum_{v \in \pi(f) \setminus \pi(k)} \psi(\lambda; \pi(f), v, \pi(s)),
    \end{equation}
    and every summand on the right-hand side is anchored.
  \end{enumerate}
  In both cases the transformation stays inside the catalogue $\Psi(\Delta_\lambda)$, depends only on $(f, k, s)$ and $\pi$, and is independent of the degree $r$.
<!-- end theorem-5 -->
<!-- proof-11: body_md -->
Admissibility follows from $\pi(f) = \pi(\operatorname{supp}(s) \cup \{k\}) = \operatorname{supp}(\pi(s)) \cup \{\pi(k)\}$. By Lemma~\ref{lem:psi-equivariance}, the pullback is
  $\psi(\lambda; \pi(f), \pi(k), \pi(s))$. By Theorem~\ref{thm:U1} on $\Delta_\lambda$, this form fails to be anchored precisely when $\operatorname{supp}(\pi(s)) = \pi(f)$ and
  $\pi(k) = \min \pi(f)$, that is, when $s_k = 1$ and $\pi(k) = \min \pi(f)$. In that
  case Lemma~\ref{lem:psi-resummation} on $\Delta_\lambda$ applied to $\psi(\lambda; \pi(f), \pi(k), \pi(s))$
  gives \eqref{eq:psi-pullback-hit}. The summands are anchored by
  Theorem~\ref{thm:U1}.
<!-- end proof-11 -->
<!-- theorem-6: body_md -->
\label{thm:U3}
  Let $(f, k, \alpha) \in \mathcal{B}(\Delta_\xi, r)$ and $\pi \in S_{D+1}$. Then
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:factorized}
    A_{\pi^{-1}}^* (w(\xi; f, k, \alpha))
    = b(\lambda; \pi(\alpha)) \, A_{\pi^{-1}}^* (\psi(\xi; f, k, \mathds{1}_{\alpha})),
  \end{equation}
  and exactly one of the following holds.
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \emph{Relabelled}. If $\alpha_k = 0$ or $\pi(k) \neq \min \pi(f)$, then
    \[ A_{\pi^{-1}}^* (w(\xi; f, k, \alpha)) = w(\lambda; \pi(f), \pi(k), \pi(\alpha)), \]
    with $(\pi(f), \pi(k), \pi(\alpha)) \in \mathcal{B}(\Delta_\lambda, r)$.
  \item \emph{Filter hit.} If $\alpha_k > 0$ and $\pi(k) = \min \pi(f)$, then
    \[ A_{\pi^{-1}}^* (w(\xi; f, k, \alpha)) = - \sum_{v \in \pi(f) \setminus \pi(k)} w(\lambda; \pi(f), v, \pi(\alpha)), \]
    with $(\pi(f), v, \pi(\alpha)) \in \mathcal{B}(\Delta_\lambda, r)$ for all $v$ of the sum.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-6 -->
<!-- proof-12: body_md -->
The pullback operation is multiplicative and relabels the barycentric scalar factor by
  Lemma~\ref{lem:bernstein}. The directional factor is transformed by Theorem~\ref{thm:psi-pullback}
  at $s = \mathds{1}_{\alpha}$, whose two cases give the two cases of the statement,
  via $\mathds{1}_{\pi(\alpha)} = \pi(\mathds{1}_{\alpha})$. Using Theorem~\ref{thm:psi-pullback}, the directional forms associated to all right-hand-side triplets are anchored, and since $|\pi(\alpha)| = r$, they are in $\mathcal{B}(\Delta_\lambda, r)$.
<!-- end proof-12 -->
<!-- theorem-7: body_md -->
\label{thm:U4}
  The families
  \[ \{A_{\pi^{-1}}^* w(\xi; f, k, \alpha) : (f, k, \alpha) \in \mathcal{B}(\Delta_\xi, r)\} \quad \text{and} \quad
     \{w(\lambda; f, k, \alpha) : (f, k, \alpha) \in \mathcal{B}(\Delta_\lambda, r)\} \]
  span the same space, namely $\mathcal{P}_r\Lambda^1 (\Delta)$. The change of basis in the reverse
  direction is obtained by applying Theorem~\ref{thm:U3} at $\pi^{-1}$.
<!-- end theorem-7 -->
<!-- proof-13: body_md -->
Write $W_\xi = \{w(\xi; \mu) : \mu \in \mathcal{B}(\Delta_\xi, r)\}$ and $W_\lambda = \{w(\lambda; \mu) : \mu \in \mathcal{B}(\Delta_\lambda, r)\}$. Theorem~\ref{thm:U3} gives $A_{\pi^{-1}}^* W_\xi \subseteq \operatorname{span} W_\lambda$ and, with the roles of $\xi$ and $\lambda$ exchanged and $\pi$ replaced by $\pi^{-1}$, $A_\pi^* W_\lambda \subseteq \operatorname{span} W_\xi$. Applying the linear map $A_{\pi^{-1}}^*$ to the second inclusion and using $A_{\pi^{-1}}^* A_\pi^* = (A_\pi A_{\pi^{-1}})^* = \mathrm{id}$,
  \[ W_\lambda = A_{\pi^{-1}}^* A_\pi^* W_\lambda \subseteq \operatorname{span} A_{\pi^{-1}}^* W_\xi \subseteq \operatorname{span} W_\lambda, \]
  so $\operatorname{span} A_{\pi^{-1}}^* W_\xi = \operatorname{span} W_\lambda = \mathcal{P}_r\Lambda^1 (\Delta)$, the last equality by Corollary~\ref{cor:basis} on $\Delta_\lambda$.
<!-- end proof-13 -->
<!-- corollary-2: body_md -->
\label{cor:sparsity}
  Define $C_\psi (\pi)$ on the index set of the directional catalogue $\Psi(\Delta_\xi)$ entrywise. For $\mu = (f, k, s)$, let
\[
  C_\psi (\pi)_{\mu \nu} =
  \begin{cases}
    +1 & \text{if } \nu = (\pi(f), \pi(k), \pi(s)) \text{ and } \mu \text{ is relabelled in Theorem~\ref{thm:psi-pullback}},\\
    -1 & \text{if } \nu = (\pi(f), v, \pi(s)),\ v \in \pi(f) \setminus \pi(k), \text{ and } \mu \text{ is a filter hit},\\
    \phantom{+}0 & \text{otherwise},
  \end{cases}
\]
so that \eqref{eq:psi-pullback-single} and \eqref{eq:psi-pullback-hit} read
$A_{\pi^{-1}}^* \psi_\mu = \sum_{\nu} C_\psi (\pi)_{\mu \nu} \, \psi_\nu (\lambda)$. Then
  \begin{equation}
    C_\psi (\pi)_{\mu \nu} \in \{-1, 0, +1\},
  \end{equation}
  each row carrying a single entry $+1$ or at most $D$ entries $-1$. $C_\psi (\pi)$ is
  independent of the degree $r$.
<!-- end corollary-2 -->
<!-- proof-14: body_md -->
By Theorem~\ref{thm:psi-pullback}, the row of $(f, k, s)$ carries either a single entry
  \[ +1 \ \text{at } (\pi(f), \pi(k), \pi(s)), \quad \text{or } \dim f \leq D \text{ entries } -1 \ \text{at } (\pi(f), v, \pi(s)), \ v \in \pi(f) \setminus \pi(k). \]
  Nothing in the definition depends on $r$.
<!-- end proof-14 -->
<!-- corollary-3: body_md -->
\label{cor:psi-inverse}
  For every $\pi \in S_{D+1}$, $C_\psi (\pi)^{-1} = C_\psi (\pi^{-1})$.
<!-- end corollary-3 -->
<!-- proof-15: body_md -->
Let $e_\nu$ denote the unit row vector at the index $\nu$, so that row $\nu$ of a matrix $C$ is $e_\nu C$. For a relabelled row, $e_{(f, k, s)} C_\psi (\pi) = e_{(\pi(f), \pi(k), \pi(s))}$, and that index is relabelled again under $\pi^{-1}$, because a hit there would require $\pi(s)_{\pi(k)} = s_k = 1$ and $\pi^{-1}(\pi(k)) = k = \min f$, which the anchoring of $(f, k, s)$ excludes by Theorem~\ref{thm:U1}, so $e_{(\pi(f), \pi(k), \pi(s))} C_\psi (\pi^{-1}) = e_{(f, k, s)}$. Let $\mu = (f, k, s)$ be a hit row, so that $s_k = 1$, $k \neq \min f$ and $\pi(k) = \min \pi(f)$. Then
  \[ e_\mu C_\psi (\pi) = - \sum_{v \in \pi(f) \setminus \pi(k)} e_{(\pi(f), v, \pi(s))}. \]
  Under $\pi^{-1}$, the index with $v = \pi(\min f)$ hits again, since $\pi^{-1}(v) = \min f$ and $\pi(s)_v = s_{\min f} = 1$, the latter because $s_k = 1$ means $k \in \operatorname{supp}(s)$, so the covering condition reads $\operatorname{supp}(s) \cup \{k\} = \operatorname{supp}(s) = f$ and thus $\min f \in \operatorname{supp}(s)$. Its row is therefore
  \[ e_{(\pi(f), \pi(\min f), \pi(s))} C_\psi (\pi^{-1}) = - \sum_{u \in f \setminus \min f} e_{(f, u, s)}, \]
  while the other indices are relabelled, $e_{(\pi(f), v, \pi(s))} C_\psi (\pi^{-1}) = e_{(f, \pi^{-1}(v), s)}$ for $v \in \pi(f) \setminus \{\pi(k), \pi(\min f)\}$, and these $\pi^{-1}(v)$ run over $f \setminus \{k, \min f\}$. Multiplying the first display by $C_\psi (\pi^{-1})$ on the right,
  \[ e_\mu C_\psi (\pi) \, C_\psi (\pi^{-1}) = - \sum_{u \in f \setminus \{k, \min f\}} e_{(f, u, s)} + \sum_{u \in f \setminus \min f} e_{(f, u, s)} = e_{(f, k, s)} = e_\mu. \]
  Hence $C_\psi (\pi) \, C_\psi (\pi^{-1}) = I$.
<!-- end proof-15 -->
<!-- corollary-4: body_md -->
\label{cor:cob}
  For $\pi \in S_{D+1}$, define $T(\pi)$ on the basis by
  \begin{equation}
    A_{\pi^{-1}}^* (w_\mu (\xi)) = \sum_{\nu \in \mathcal{B}(\Delta_\lambda, r)} T(\pi)_{\mu \nu} \, w_\nu (\lambda),
    \quad \mu \in \mathcal{B}(\Delta_\xi, r).
  \end{equation}
  Then $T(\pi)$ is well defined, its entries lie in $\{-1, 0, +1\}$, each row
  carries a single entry $+1$ or at most $D$ entries $-1$, and
  $T(\pi)^{-1} = T(\pi^{-1})$. Unlike the catalogue matrix $C_\psi (\pi)$, the matrix
  $T(\pi)$ depends on $r$, but only through its index set $\mathcal{B}(\Delta_\xi, r)$.
<!-- end corollary-4 -->
<!-- proof-16: body_md -->
$\mathcal{B}(\Delta_\lambda, r)$ is a basis by Corollary~\ref{cor:basis}, so the expansion exists and is
  unique, and $T(\pi)$ is well defined. Theorem~\ref{thm:U3} exhibits the expansion of every
  row, with a single entry $+1$ at $(\pi(f), \pi(k), \pi(\alpha))$ or $\dim f \leq D$ entries
  $-1$ at the triplets $(\pi(f), v, \pi(\alpha))$, $v \in \pi(f) \setminus \pi(k)$. Composing Theorem~\ref{thm:U3}
  at $\pi$ and at $\pi^{-1}$, as in Theorem~\ref{thm:U4}, gives $T(\pi) \, T(\pi^{-1}) = I$.
<!-- end proof-16 -->
<!-- remark-8: body_md -->
In practice the change of basis can be applied through the factorisation
  \eqref{eq:factorized}. The catalogue $\Psi(\Delta_\xi)$, the matrices $C_\psi (\pi)$, and the
  applicable case of Theorem~\ref{thm:psi-pullback} for each catalogue form can be precomputable once for a given $K$ and $D$. Per basis
  function, the case test reads the stored exponent $\alpha_k$ and compares
  $\pi(k)$ with $\min \pi(f)$, at small and constant cost. The scalar factor
  undergoes the index permutation $\alpha \mapsto \pi(\alpha)$. Only the directional factors
  require change-of-basis. Since the matrix $T(\pi)$ of
  Corollary~\ref{cor:cob} is known in closed form, it is not necessary to allocate it to apply its action.
<!-- end remark-8 -->
<!-- remark-9: body_md -->
The numerically computed transformation matrices mentioned in the introduction act on
  the assembled shape functions, treating the relocation of the
  multi-exponent and the pullback of the 1-form factors together. Their blocks thus
  grow with the degree, and the structure exhibited here is invisible to them.
  The factorisation \eqref{eq:factorized} separates the two. The family of barycentric monomials is mapped to itself by every relabelling, each monomial to a single monomial (Lemma~\ref{lem:bernstein}); the catalogue is not, and the whole change of basis is carried by the $r$-independent matrix $C_\psi (\pi)$ with entries in $\{-1, 0, +1\}$.
<!-- end remark-9 -->
<!-- definition-5: body_md -->
\label{def:trimmed-spanning}
  $\mathcal{S}^-(\Delta_\xi, r)$ is the set of triplets $(f, e, \alpha)$ with $\dim f \geq 1$, an ordered
  pair $e = (e_1, e_2)$ of labels of $f$ with $e_1 \neq e_2$, $|\alpha| = r - 1$ and
  $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha) \cup \{e_1, e_2\} = f$. To each is associated the 1-form
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:trimmed-w}
    w(\xi; f, e, \alpha) = b(\xi; \alpha) \, \varphi(\xi; e_1, e_2),
  \end{equation}
  with $\varphi$ the Whitney 1-form \eqref{eq:whitney}, that is $\varphi(\xi; e_1, e_2) = \xi_{e_1} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_{e_2} - \xi_{e_2} \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_{e_1}$.
<!-- end definition-5 -->
<!-- remark-10: body_md -->
We deliberately do not impose $e_1 < e_2$ in the spanning set, in contrast to
  the convention of \cite{ArnoldFalkWinther2009}. Keeping the pair orders and the
  alternation $\varphi(\xi; e_2, e_1) = -\varphi(\xi; e_1, e_2)$ enables simplifying the upcoming relabelling theorem by using the $\varepsilon$ symbol to handle sign changes.
  Note also that $\dim f \geq 1$ is guaranteed by $\{e_1, e_2\} \subseteq f$. So as in the full
  space, vertices own no basis functions.
<!-- end remark-10 -->
<!-- theorem-8: body_md -->
\label{thm:trimmed-spanning}
  $\operatorname{span} \mathcal{S}^-(\Delta_\xi, r) = \mathcal{P}_r^{-}\Lambda^1 (\Delta)$ for every $r \geq 1$.
<!-- end theorem-8 -->
<!-- proof-17: body_md -->
Every element of
  $\mathcal{S}^-(\Delta_\xi, r)$ is of the form $\xi^\alpha \varphi(\xi; i, j)$ with $|\alpha| = r - 1$, hence lies
  in $\mathcal{P}_r^{-}\Lambda^1$ by \eqref{eq:trimmed-space}. Conversely if $f, (i, j), \alpha$ is an admissible argument in Definition~\ref{def:trimmed-spanning}, then the generator $\xi^\alpha \varphi(\xi; i, j)$
  of \eqref{eq:trimmed-space} equals $w(\xi; f, (i, j), \alpha)$ since $f = \operatorname{supp}(\alpha) \cup \{i, j\}$.
<!-- end proof-17 -->
<!-- definition-6: body_md -->
\label{def:trimmed-filter}
  A pair $(f, e)$ is \emph{anchored} if $e_1 < e_2$ and $e_1 = \min f$.
  $\mathcal{B}^-(\Delta_\xi, r) \subseteq \mathcal{S}^-(\Delta_\xi, r)$ consists of the triplets $(f, e, \alpha)$ whose
  pair is anchored.
<!-- end definition-6 -->
<!-- theorem-9: body_md -->
\label{thm:T1}
  A triplet $(f, e, \alpha) \in \mathcal{S}^-(\Delta_\xi, r)$ has anchored pair
  if and only if $e_1 < e_2$ and
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:trimmed-filter}
    (\mathds{1}_{\alpha})_i = 0 \quad \text{for all} \quad i < e_1.
  \end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-9 -->
<!-- proof-18: body_md -->
If the pair is anchored, then $e_1 = \min f < e_2$, and every
  $i < e_1$ lies outside $f$, hence outside $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha) \subseteq f$, so both
  conditions hold. Conversely, assume $e_1 < e_2$ and \eqref{eq:trimmed-filter}.
  Every element of $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha)$ is then at least $e_1$, and $e_2 > e_1$, so
  $\min f = \min(\operatorname{supp}(\alpha) \cup \{e_1, e_2\}) = e_1$ and the pair is anchored.
<!-- end proof-18 -->
<!-- remark-11: body_md -->
Unlike for the full space, the filter-hit condition of the trimmed space is independent of $\alpha$. This
  $\alpha$-independence propagates to the pullback (Theorem~\ref{thm:T3}), so that all basis
  functions sharing a pair $(f, e)$ transform alike.
<!-- end remark-11 -->
<!-- lemma-6: body_md -->
\label{lem:pou}
  For any three distinct labels $a, b, c$,
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:pou}
    \xi_a \, \varphi(\xi; b, c) = \xi_b \, \varphi(\xi; a, c) - \xi_c \, \varphi(\xi; a, b).
  \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-6 -->
<!-- proof-19: body_md -->
Expanding against \eqref{eq:whitney}, both sides equal
  $\xi_a \xi_b \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_c - \xi_a \xi_c \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_b$ after pairwise
  cancellation. The identity is equivalent to the cyclic relation
  $\xi_a \varphi(b, c) + \xi_b \varphi(c, a) + \xi_c \varphi(a, b) = 0$ from
  \cite[Prop.~3.5]{RapettiBossavit2009}.
<!-- end proof-19 -->
<!-- theorem-10: body_md -->
\label{thm:T2}
  Let $(f, e, \alpha) \in \mathcal{S}^-(\Delta_\xi, r) \setminus \mathcal{B}^-(\Delta_\xi, r)$ with $e_1 < e_2$, and set
  $m \doteq \min f$. Then $m < e_1$, $\alpha_m > 0$ and
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:trimmed-decomp}
    w(\xi; f, (e_1, e_2), \alpha)
    = w(\xi; f, (m, e_2), \rho(m, e_1) \circ \alpha) - w(\xi; f, (m, e_1), \rho(m, e_2) \circ \alpha),
  \end{equation}
  and both triplets on the right-hand side belong to $\mathcal{B}^-(\Delta_\xi, r)$.
<!-- end theorem-10 -->
<!-- proof-20: body_md -->
Since the pair $(f, e)$ is not anchored, $m = \min f \notin \{e_1, e_2\}$, so the covering condition gives
  $\alpha_m > 0$. To obtain \eqref{eq:trimmed-decomp}, instantiate \eqref{eq:pou} at $(a, b, c) = (m, e_1, e_2)$, multiply
  by $b(\xi; \alpha) / \xi_m$, and use
  \begin{equation}
    \frac{b(\xi; \alpha)}{\xi_m} \cdot \xi_{e_1} = b(\xi; \rho(m, e_1) \circ \alpha), \quad
    \frac{b(\xi; \alpha)}{\xi_m} \cdot \xi_{e_2} = b(\xi; \rho(m, e_2) \circ \alpha),
  \end{equation}
  which are polynomial identities because $\alpha_m \geq 1$. The right-hand side triplets belong to $\mathcal{S}^-$ since $\rho$ preserves the multi-index moduli, and the index exchanges preserve the cover $f = \operatorname{supp}(\alpha) \cup e$. The new pairs are anchored since $m = \min f$.
<!-- end proof-20 -->
<!-- lemma-7: body_md -->
\label{lem:trimmed-count}
  A face $f$ with $d = \dim f$ owns $d \binom{r}{d}$ different triplets of $\mathcal{B}^-(\Delta_\xi, r)$, and the cardinality of the whole set is
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:trimmed-count}
    \# \mathcal{B}^-(\Delta_\xi, r) = r \binom{r + D}{D - 1} = \dim \mathcal{P}_r^{-}\Lambda^1.
  \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-7 -->
<!-- proof-21: body_md -->
Fix $f$ with $|f| = d + 1$. By Definition~\ref{def:trimmed-filter} the triplets owned by $f$ have
  $e_1 = \min f$ and $e_2 \in f \setminus \min f$, giving $d$ choices of pair. For each, the
  multi-exponents completing an admissible triplet have $|\alpha| = r - 1$, must be positive on the $d - 1$ labels
  of $f \setminus \{e_1, e_2\}$, and may be positive on the two labels $e_1, e_2$. The map
  \[ \alpha \mapsto \beta \doteq \alpha - \sum_{i \in f \setminus \{e_1, e_2\}} 1_i \]
  is a bijection from these exponents onto the multi-exponents $\beta$ with
  $\operatorname{supp}(\beta) \subseteq f$ and $|\beta| = (r - 1) - (d - 1) = r - d$, and there are
  $\binom{(r - d) + d}{d} = \binom{r}{d}$ such $\beta$. This is the number of ways to
  distribute $r - d$ units over the $d + 1$ labels of $f$.
    The absorption identity $d \binom{r}{d} = r \binom{r - 1}{d - 1}$ rewrites this count as $r \binom{r - 1}{d - 1}$. Summing over the $\binom{D + 1}{d + 1}$ faces of dimension $d$ and using Vandermonde's identity $\sum_{d = 1}^{D} \binom{D + 1}{d + 1} \binom{r - 1}{d - 1} = \binom{r + D}{D - 1}$,
  \[ \# \mathcal{B}^-(\Delta_\xi, r) = r \sum_{d = 1}^{D} \binom{D + 1}{d + 1} \binom{r - 1}{d - 1} = r \binom{r + D}{D - 1}, \]
  which is $\dim \mathcal{P}_r^{-}\Lambda^1$ by \eqref{eq:trimmed-space}.
<!-- end proof-21 -->
<!-- corollary-5: body_md -->
\label{cor:trimmed-basis}
  $\mathcal{B}^-(\Delta_\xi, r)$ is a basis of $\mathcal{P}_r^{-}\Lambda^1 (\Delta)$.
<!-- end corollary-5 -->
<!-- proof-22: body_md -->
Alternation maps the $e_1 > e_2$ spanning elements to their sorted negatives,
  and Theorem~\ref{thm:T2} expresses every sorted element of $\mathcal{S}^- \setminus \mathcal{B}^-$ in
  $\operatorname{span} \mathcal{B}^-$. Hence $\operatorname{span} \mathcal{B}^- = \operatorname{span} \mathcal{S}^- = \mathcal{P}_r^{-}\Lambda^1$ by
  Theorem~\ref{thm:trimmed-spanning}, and Lemma~\ref{lem:trimmed-count} concludes by
  cardinality. In particular, distinct triplets of $\mathcal{B}^-(\Delta_\xi, r)$ give distinct forms.
<!-- end proof-22 -->
<!-- lemma-8: body_md -->
\label{lem:trimmed-trace}
  Let $(f, e, \alpha) \in \mathcal{S}^-(\Delta_\xi, r)$ and let $g$ be a face of $\Delta_\xi$ that does not
  contain $f$. Then $\operatorname{tr}_g w(\xi; f, e, \alpha) = 0$.
<!-- end lemma-8 -->
<!-- proof-23: body_md -->
As in Lemma~\ref{lem:trace}, if some $i \in \operatorname{supp}(\alpha)$ lies outside $g$ the Bernstein factor
  vanishes identically on $g$. Otherwise $\operatorname{supp}(\alpha) \subseteq g$, and since
  $f = \operatorname{supp}(\alpha) \cup \{e_1, e_2\}$ is not contained in $g$, at least one of the two
  labels $e_1, e_2$ lies outside $g$. For that label $\xi_{e_i}$ vanishes on $g$ and
  $\operatorname{tr}_g \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_{e_i} = 0$, so both terms of \eqref{eq:whitney} have vanishing
  trace.
<!-- end proof-23 -->
<!-- theorem-11: body_md -->
\label{thm:phi-equivariance}
  For distinct labels $e_1 \neq e_2$ and $\pi \in S_{D+1}$, writing
  $\pi(e) = (\pi(e_1), \pi(e_2))$,
  \begin{equation}
    A_{\pi^{-1}}^* (\varphi(\xi; e_1, e_2)) = \varphi(\lambda; \pi(e_1), \pi(e_2))
    = \varepsilon(\pi(e)) \, \varphi(\lambda; \pi(e)^{\uparrow}).
  \end{equation}
<!-- end theorem-11 -->
<!-- proof-24: body_md -->
The pullback $A_{\pi^{-1}}^*$ maps $\xi_{e_i} \mapsto \lambda_{\pi(e_i)}$ and
  $\mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \xi_{e_i} \mapsto \mathop{}\!\mathrm{d} \lambda_{\pi(e_i)}$, and the second equality is the alternation of
  $\varphi$.
<!-- end proof-24 -->
<!-- theorem-12: body_md -->
\label{thm:T3}
  Let $(f, e, \alpha) \in \mathcal{B}^-(\Delta_\xi, r)$, so that $e_1 = \min f < e_2$, and let
  $\pi \in S_{D+1}$. Write $\varepsilon = \varepsilon(\pi(e))$, $(e_1^\pi, e_2^\pi) = \pi(e)^{\uparrow}$ and
  $m^\pi = \min \pi(f)$. Then
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:trimmed-pullback-raw}
    A_{\pi^{-1}}^* (w(\xi; f, e, \alpha)) = \varepsilon \, b(\lambda; \pi(\alpha)) \, \varphi(\lambda; \pi(e)^{\uparrow}),
  \end{equation}
  and exactly one of the following holds.
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item \emph{Relabelled}. If $e_1^\pi = m^\pi$, equivalently if
    $\pi^{-1}(m^\pi) \in \{e_1, e_2\}$, the pair $(\pi(f), \pi(e)^{\uparrow})$ is anchored and
    \[ A_{\pi^{-1}}^* w(\xi; f, e, \alpha) = \varepsilon \, w(\lambda; \pi(f), \pi(e)^{\uparrow}, \pi(\alpha)), \]
    with $(\pi(f), \pi(e)^{\uparrow}, \pi(\alpha)) \in \mathcal{B}^-(\Delta_\lambda, r)$.
  \item \emph{Filter hit.} Otherwise, and independently of $\alpha$,
    \begin{equation}\label{eq:trimmed-pullback-hit}
      \begin{aligned}
        A_{\pi^{-1}}^* (w(\xi; f, e, \alpha)) = \varepsilon \bigl( &\, w(\lambda; \pi(f), (m^\pi, e_2^\pi), \rho(m^\pi, e_1^\pi) \circ \pi(\alpha))\\
        - &\, w(\lambda; \pi(f), (m^\pi, e_1^\pi), \rho(m^\pi, e_2^\pi) \circ \pi(\alpha)) \bigr),
      \end{aligned}
    \end{equation}
    with both triplets on the right in $\mathcal{B}^-(\Delta_\lambda, r)$.
  \end{enumerate}
<!-- end theorem-12 -->
<!-- proof-25: body_md -->
The pullback operation is multiplicative, relabels the scalar factors by
  Lemma~\ref{lem:bernstein}, and rotates the Whitney forms by Theorem~\ref{thm:phi-equivariance},
  which gives \eqref{eq:trimmed-pullback-raw}. $|\pi(\alpha)| = r - 1$ and
  $\pi(\operatorname{supp}(\alpha) \cup \{e_1, e_2\}) = \operatorname{supp}(\pi(\alpha)) \cup \{\pi(e_1), \pi(e_2)\}$ ensure that
  $(\pi(f), \pi(e)^{\uparrow}, \pi(\alpha))$ belongs to the spanning set. By Definition~\ref{def:trimmed-filter} on $\Delta_\lambda$, this
  triplet is in $\mathcal{B}^-(\Delta_\lambda, r)$ iff its pair is anchored, that is, iff
  $e_1^\pi = m^\pi$. Otherwise, the remaining statements result from applying Theorem~\ref{thm:T2} on $\Delta_\lambda$ to
  $(\pi(f), \pi(e)^{\uparrow}, \pi(\alpha))$, since the face minimum is $m^\pi$.
<!-- end proof-25 -->
<!-- remark-12: body_md -->
\label{rem:no-hits}
  For $r = 1$ the exponent vanishes, so $f = \{e_1, e_2\}$ and
  $\min \pi(f) = \min(\pi(e_1), \pi(e_2))$. No filter hit can occur, and Theorem~\ref{thm:T3}
  reduces to $A_{\pi^{-1}}^* \varphi(\xi; e) = \varepsilon(\pi(e)) \, \varphi(\lambda; \pi(e)^{\uparrow})$, the classical
  alternating sign rule for Whitney edge elements \cite{LohiKettunen2021}. In the
  language of \cite{BerchenkoKogan2024}, the lowest-order Whitney basis is invariant up
  to sign \cite[Lemma 6]{Licht2023symmetry}.
<!-- end remark-12 -->
<!-- theorem-13: body_md -->
\label{thm:T4}
  The families
  \[ \{A_{\pi^{-1}}^* w(\xi; f, e, \alpha) : (f, e, \alpha) \in \mathcal{B}^-(\Delta_\xi, r)\} \quad \text{and} \quad
     \{w(\lambda; f, e, \alpha) : (f, e, \alpha) \in \mathcal{B}^-(\Delta_\lambda, r)\} \]
  both span $\mathcal{P}_r^{-}\Lambda^1 (\Delta)$. The reverse change of basis is obtained
  by applying Theorem~\ref{thm:T3} at $\pi^{-1}$.
<!-- end theorem-13 -->
<!-- proof-26: body_md -->
As for Theorem~\ref{thm:U4}, with Theorem~\ref{thm:T3} and Corollary~\ref{cor:trimmed-basis} in place of Theorem~\ref{thm:U3} and Corollary~\ref{cor:basis}.
<!-- end proof-26 -->
<!-- corollary-6: body_md -->
\label{cor:trimmed-sparsity}
  Define $C_\varphi (\pi)$ on the catalogue of Whitney forms with sorted pairs by
  $A_{\pi^{-1}}^* \varphi_\mu = \sum_{\nu} C_\varphi (\pi)_{\mu \nu} \, \varphi_\nu (\lambda)$. Then $C_\varphi (\pi)$ is a
  signed permutation matrix with $C_\varphi (\pi)^{-1} = C_\varphi (\pi^{-1})$, independent of
  the degree $r$.
<!-- end corollary-6 -->
<!-- proof-27: body_md -->
The statements restate Theorem~\ref{thm:phi-equivariance}, Theorem~\ref{thm:T3} and Theorem~\ref{thm:T4}.
<!-- end proof-27 -->
<!-- corollary-7: body_md -->
\label{cor:trimmed-cob}
  For $\pi \in S_{D+1}$, define $T(\pi)$ on the basis by
  \begin{equation}
    A_{\pi^{-1}}^* (w_\mu (\xi)) = \sum_{\nu \in \mathcal{B}^-(\Delta_\lambda, r)} T(\pi)_{\mu \nu} \, w_\nu (\lambda),
    \quad \mu \in \mathcal{B}^-(\Delta_\xi, r).
  \end{equation}
  Then $T(\pi)$ is well defined, each row
  contains a single non-zero entry $\varepsilon(\pi(e)) \in \{-1, +1\}$ or exactly two non-zero entries,
  $\varepsilon(\pi(e))$ and $-\varepsilon(\pi(e))$, and $T(\pi)^{-1} = T(\pi^{-1})$. As in Sect.~\ref{sec:full}, the
  matrix depends on $r$ only through its index set $\mathcal{B}^-(\Delta_\xi, r)$.
<!-- end corollary-7 -->
<!-- proof-28: body_md -->
$\mathcal{B}^-(\Delta_\lambda, r)$ is a basis by Corollary~\ref{cor:trimmed-basis}, so the expansion is
  unique and $T(\pi)$ is well defined. Theorem~\ref{thm:T3} exhibits the expansion of every
  row, a single entry $\varepsilon(\pi(e))$ at $(\pi(f), \pi(e)^{\uparrow}, \pi(\alpha))$ or the two entries of
  \eqref{eq:trimmed-pullback-hit}. Composing Theorem~\ref{thm:T3} at $\pi$ and at $\pi^{-1}$ gives $T(\pi) \, T(\pi^{-1}) = I$.
<!-- end proof-28 -->
<!-- remark-13: body_md -->
\label{rem:standard-basis}
  As noted in Sect.~\ref{sec:trimmed-basis}, $\mathcal{B}^-(\Delta_\xi, r)$ is the geometrically decomposed basis of $\mathcal{P}_r^{-}\Lambda^1$ from \cite[Section 9]{ArnoldFalkWinther2009}. The signed two-term transformation law of Theorem~\ref{thm:T3} is therefore a property of
  the standard basis of the literature.
  To the best of our knowledge it has gone unremarked; \cite{ArnoldFalkWinther2009} constructs the bases and their decomposition but does not consider the pullback of basis functions under vertex relabellings.
<!-- end remark-13 -->
<!-- remark-14: body_md -->
In practice the change of basis can be applied through
  \eqref{eq:trimmed-pullback-raw} and \eqref{eq:trimmed-pullback-hit}. The sign $\varepsilon$, the sorted pair, and the anchoring
  test $\pi^{-1}(\min \pi(f)) \in \{e_1, e_2\}$ are pair-level data, independent of $r$
  and of $\alpha$. The scalar factor undergoes the index permutation
  $\alpha \mapsto \pi(\alpha)$ and, only in the hit case, the two shifts $\rho$.
<!-- end remark-14 -->
<!-- lemma-9: body_md -->
The family $\{\sigma_p\}$ is a basis of the dual space $(\mathcal{P}_r\Lambda^1)'$, respectively
  $(\mathcal{P}_r^{-}\Lambda^1)'$; equivalently, the degree-of-freedom set is unisolvent.
<!-- end lemma-9 -->
<!-- proof-29: body_md -->
If $\sum_p c_p \, \sigma_p = 0$, evaluation at $w(\xi; q)$ gives $c_q = 0$ for
  every triplet $q$ of the basis, so the family is linearly independent. Its
  cardinality is $\dim \mathcal{P}_r\Lambda^1$ by \eqref{eq:count}, respectively $\dim \mathcal{P}_r^{-}\Lambda^1$ by
  \eqref{eq:trimmed-count}, so it is a basis of the dual space.
<!-- end proof-29 -->
<!-- definition-7: body_md -->
\label{def:identification}
    Let $(f_+, \nu_+)$ and $(f_-, \nu_-)$ be rotated functions of the cells $K_+$ and $K_-$. They are \emph{identified}, $(f_+, \nu_+) \sim (f_-, \nu_-)$, if
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:identification}
    \operatorname{ltg}_{K_+}(\pi_+^{-1}(f_+)) = \operatorname{ltg}_{K_-}(\pi_-^{-1}(f_-)) \qquad \text{and} \qquad p_{f_+}(\nu_+) = p_{f_-}(\nu_-).
  \end{equation}
<!-- end definition-7 -->
<!-- corollary-8: body_md -->
\label{cor:conformity}\label{cor:assembly}
    Let $K_\pm$ share the mesh face $F$.
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item A rotated function of $K_+$ owned by a mesh face $G \subseteq F$ is identified with exactly one rotated function of $K_-$, and that function is owned by $G$.
  \item Identified rotated functions have the same trace on $F$.
  \item Rotated functions of $K_\pm$ owned by faces not contained in $F$ have zero trace on $F$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Consequently, the space assembled by \eqref{eq:identification} is $H \Lambda^1$-conforming.
<!-- end corollary-8 -->
<!-- proof-30: body_md -->
(1) Let $g_\pm$ be the sorted labels of $G$ in $K_\pm$, so that $\operatorname{ltg}_{K_\pm}(\pi_\pm^{-1}(g_\pm)) = G$. By \eqref{eq:identification}, $(g_+, \nu_+)$ is identified with the functions $(g_-, \nu_-)$ of $K_-$ such that $p_{g_-}(\nu_-) = p_{g_+}(\nu_+)$, and with no function owned by another face. Since $p_{g_-}$ is a bijection onto $\{0, \dots, \# \mathcal{B}_{g_-} - 1\}$ and $\# \mathcal{B}_{g_-} = \# \mathcal{B}_{g_+}$, there is exactly one such $\nu_-$.
  (2) Both $g_+$ and $g_-$ list the vertices of $G$ by increasing global vertex index, hence the increasing bijection $\sigma_{g_+ \to g_-}$ maps the label of each vertex of $G$ in $K_+$ to its label in $K_-$. The barycentric coordinate of a vertex of $G$ restricted to $F$ is intrinsic to $F$, so $\lambda^+_a = \lambda^-_{\sigma_{g_+ \to g_-}(a)}$ on $F$ for every $a \in g_+$. Since \eqref{eq:w} and \eqref{eq:trimmed-w} involve only the labels of the owning face, $(g_+, \nu_+)$ and $(g_-, \iota_{g_+ \to g_-}(\nu_+))$ have the same trace on $F$. This is the function of (1), owned by $G$ and $p_{g_-}(\iota_{g_+ \to g_-}(\nu_+)) = p_{g_+}(\nu_+)$ by \eqref{eq:position-compat}.
  (3) This is Lemmas~\ref{lem:trace} and~\ref{lem:trimmed-trace}.
  Consequently, the trace on $F$ of a glued basis function is either zero on both sides, by (3), or the common trace of two identified functions, by (1) and (2); it is single valued on every mesh face.
<!-- end proof-30 -->
<!-- remark-15: body_md -->
Julia, and every Gridap
  interface underneath (Bernstein term identifiers, polytope face tables, vertex
  numbering), is 1-based, so the code labels the vertices $1, \dots, D+1$ instead of
  $0, \dots, D$. All label logic is order-theoretic (comparisons and minima), so the
  translation is the uniform shift by one.
<!-- end remark-15 -->
<!-- lemma-10: body_md -->
\label{lem:shift-ratio}
  For distinct labels $i \neq j$ and a multi-exponent $\alpha$ with $\alpha_i > 0$,
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:shift-ratio}
    c(\alpha) / c(\rho(i, j) \circ \alpha) = (\alpha_j + 1) / \alpha_i.
  \end{equation}
<!-- end lemma-10 -->
<!-- proof-31: body_md -->
The shift preserves $|\alpha|$, and replaces $\alpha_i !$ by $(\alpha_i - 1)!$ and $\alpha_j !$ by
  $(\alpha_j + 1)!$.
<!-- end proof-31 -->
<!-- corollary-9: body_md -->
\label{cor:bernstein-decomp}
  With the notation of Theorem~\ref{thm:T2},
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:bernstein-decomp}
    \begin{aligned}
      \tilde{w}(\xi; f, (e_1, e_2), \alpha) =
        &\ \frac{\alpha_{e_1} + 1}{\alpha_m} \, \tilde{w}(\xi; f, (m, e_2), \rho(m, e_1) \circ \alpha)\\
      - &\ \frac{\alpha_{e_2} + 1}{\alpha_m} \, \tilde{w}(\xi; f, (m, e_1), \rho(m, e_2) \circ \alpha).
    \end{aligned}
  \end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-9 -->
<!-- proof-32: body_md -->
Multiply \eqref{eq:trimmed-decomp} by $c(\alpha)$ and use Lemma~\ref{lem:shift-ratio} at $(m, e_1)$
  and $(m, e_2)$, both admissible because $\alpha_m > 0$.
<!-- end proof-32 -->
<!-- corollary-10: body_md -->
\label{cor:bernstein-pullback}
  With the notation of Theorem~\ref{thm:T3}, write $\beta = \pi(\alpha)$. The relabelled case is
  \[ A_{\pi^{-1}}^* (\tilde{w}(\xi; f, e, \alpha)) = \varepsilon \, \tilde{w}(\lambda; \pi(f), \pi(e)^{\uparrow}, \beta), \]
  and the filter hit is
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:bernstein-pullback-hit}
    \begin{aligned}
      A_{\pi^{-1}}^* (\tilde{w}(\xi; f, e, \alpha)) = \varepsilon \bigl(
        &\ \frac{\beta_{e_1^\pi} + 1}{\beta_{m^\pi}} \,
          \tilde{w}(\lambda; \pi(f), (m^\pi, e_2^\pi), \rho(m^\pi, e_1^\pi) \circ \beta)\\
      - &\ \frac{\beta_{e_2^\pi} + 1}{\beta_{m^\pi}} \,
          \tilde{w}(\lambda; \pi(f), (m^\pi, e_1^\pi), \rho(m^\pi, e_2^\pi) \circ \beta) \bigr).
    \end{aligned}
  \end{equation}
<!-- end corollary-10 -->
<!-- proof-33: body_md -->
The multinomial factor $c$ is invariant under any permutation of the entries of
  $\alpha$, so $c(\pi(\alpha)) = c(\alpha)$ and \eqref{eq:trimmed-pullback-raw} holds with $\tilde{b}$ and
  $\tilde{w}$ in place of $b$ and $w$. Which of the two cases holds is a property
  of the pair, as in Theorem~\ref{thm:T3}. The hit case then results from applying
  Corollary~\ref{cor:bernstein-decomp} on $\Delta_\lambda$ to $(\pi(f), \pi(e)^{\uparrow}, \beta)$.
<!-- end proof-33 -->
<!-- corollary-11: body_md -->
\label{cor:bernstein-cob}
  Define $\tilde{T}(\pi)$ as in Corollary~\ref{cor:trimmed-cob} with $\tilde{w}$ in place of $w$, and
  let $S$ be the diagonal matrix whose entry at $\mu = (f, e, \alpha)$ is $c(\alpha)$. Then
  \begin{equation}\label{eq:bernstein-cob}
    \tilde{T}(\pi) = S \, T(\pi) \, S^{-1}.
  \end{equation}
  Consequently, $\tilde{T}(\pi)$ has the sparsity of $T(\pi)$, and $\tilde{T}(\pi)^{-1}
  = \tilde{T}(\pi^{-1})$.
<!-- end corollary-11 -->
<!-- proof-34: body_md -->
$\tilde{w}_\mu = c(\alpha) \, w_\mu$ on both $\Delta_\xi$ and $\Delta_\lambda$, so \eqref{eq:bernstein-cob}
  restates the expansion of Corollary~\ref{cor:trimmed-cob}. A diagonal change of basis
  preserves the sparsity and the identity $T(\pi)^{-1} = T(\pi^{-1})$. The entries
  follow from Corollary~\ref{cor:bernstein-pullback}.
<!-- end proof-34 -->
